chapter_title: Objectives, Uses, and Products of Site Characterization Investigations

sections.title: General Objectives for Site Characterization
sections.summary: Investigations for site characterization address eight objectives: (1) stratigraphy — identify and characterize soil/rock types and develop cross-sections; (2) groundwater conditions; (3) design parameters — develop reliable estimates; (4) constructability — characterize conditions affecting methods, schedule, and risk; (5) hazard identification — identify and characterize geotechnical hazards; (6) suitability — characterize soil/rock for specific uses; (7) condition assessment and performance monitoring; and (8) location and alignment decisions. Test method suitability depends on the objective: tests for hazard identification may be poorly suited for design parameters, and vice versa.
sections.body:
Investigations are generally performed to address one or more specific objectives: (1) Stratigraphy — identify and qualitatively characterize soil/rock types, define discrete strata, develop cross-sections; (2) Groundwater Conditions — characterize groundwater conditions and potential impacts for design, construction, and operation; (3) Design Parameters — develop reliable estimates for relevant design parameters for design; (4) Constructability — characterize conditions affecting construction methods, schedule, and risks; (5) Hazard Identification — identify and characterize geotechnical hazards; (6) Suitability — characterize soil/rock for specific uses (fill, aggregate); (7) Condition Assessment and Performance Monitoring — assess current conditions and document performance; (8) Location and Alignment — qualitatively characterize conditions to inform location/alignment decisions.

The term 'hazard' refers to a condition with potential to negatively impact construction or operation; 'risk' combines the likelihood of a hazard impacting the project with potential consequences (costs). Suitability of different investigations is tied to objectives — tests for profiling or constructability may be poorly suited for design parameter characterization, and conversely.
key_points: 8 investigation objectives: stratigraphy, groundwater, design parameters, constructability, hazard ID, suitability, monitoring, location/alignment
Hazard = potential to negatively impact construction/operations; Risk = likelihood × consequences
Test method suitability depends on the specific objective — profiling tests may be poorly suited for design parameter characterization

sections.title: Classes of Site Characterization Investigations
sections.summary: Five investigation classes: (1) desk studies — gather existing information before field work; (2) preliminary investigations — sparse borings, disturbed samples, index tests, geophysical scanning; (3) design investigations — targeted after alignment/grade set; confirm stratigraphy and establish reliable design parameters; (4) borrow site investigations — suitability of fill sources; (5) forensic investigations — identify cause of problems. Design-build projects require more extensive preliminary data than standard bid-build; design-builder performs final investigations after contract award.
sections.body:
Desk studies: Critical first step; gather historical records, performance records, geologic reports, maps (geologic, soil survey, topographic, utility), aerial photographs, satellite imagery, consultation with colleagues, and applicable laws/regulations. Inform planning and scoping, location/alignment, and early hazard identification.

Preliminary investigations: Early project stage; support planning and qualitative preliminary design; sparse subsurface investigations (shallow borings, test pits, in situ soundings); bulk/disturbed samples for index property tests; geophysical scanning methods (seismic reflection/refraction, MASW, electrical resistivity) to interpret conditions between sparse borings.

Design investigations: After alignment/grade set and specific structure locations established; more rigorous and targeted; advanced boring, sampling, and testing techniques; confirm/refine stratigraphy and establish reliable design parameters; may include specialized boring techniques, advanced lab testing, in situ field tests, and geophysical methods. Special investigations address specific challenges (soft foundation embankments, large bridges, specific hazards).

Borrow site investigations: Characterize stratigraphy and general type; disturbed samples and index tests; test pits; compaction specimens when source is confirmed suitable.

Forensic investigations: Identify cause of failure; directed at specific locations; advanced techniques; often performed with urgency; may include location of sliding surface, groundwater conditions at time of failure, and parameters for remedial design.

Design-build investigations: Owner provides data sufficient for bidders to develop designs and estimate costs. Data must generally characterize stratigraphy, soil/rock properties, and groundwater — more extensive than routine preliminary but not as rigorous as final design. Selected design-build organization performs additional investigations after award.
key_points: Desk study is the critical first step — always performed before field work
Preliminary: sparse borings, disturbed samples, index tests, geophysical scanning
Design: targeted, advanced boring/sampling/testing; confirms stratigraphy and establishes reliable design parameters
Design-build: owner provides more extensive preliminary data; design-builder conducts final investigations after award
Forensic: directed at specific failure locations; advanced methods; often performed with urgency

sections.title: Geotechnical Reporting Documents and Benefits
sections.summary: Four geotechnical reporting documents: (1) field investigation logs — factual observations only; (2) geotechnical data reports — investigations plus factual test results; no interpretations; may be legally binding in contract documents; (3) geotechnical design reports — include interpretations of stratigraphy, design parameters, hazards, and recommendations; not typically in bid documents; (4) geotechnical baseline reports (GBR) — contractually binding interpretation; basis for claims and change orders. Benefits: more reliable design parameters, early hazard identification, and reduced contractor risk.
sections.body:
Field investigation logs: Most common products; include boring logs, test pit logs, in situ testing logs (CPT, DMT, VST), groundwater monitoring logs, and geophysical survey reports. Should include important field observations (difficult drilling, loss of drilling fluid, rod drops indicating karst, borehole stability problems).

Geotechnical data reports: Include description of investigations, field investigation logs, and laboratory/field test results. Include only factual data — no interpretations or recommendations. Because only factual information, may be included in project plans and bid documents; may be legally binding. Part of design-build contracts.

Geotechnical design reports: Include detailed site description plus analysis methods, design results, interpretations, and recommendations. Include stratigraphy interpretations, groundwater conditions, geotechnical hazards and risks, and design parameter values. Often the 'complete' characterization product. Generally not included in bid documents due to subjective interpretations.

Geotechnical Baseline Reports (GBR): Special product for design-build projects (ASCE 2007). Establishes contractually binding baseline for ground conditions accepted by all parties before construction. Basis for claims and change orders.

Benefits of site characterization: (1) More reliable design parameters allow more efficient (less conservative) design; (2) Early hazard identification when it is easier and cheaper to address; (3) Accurate stratigraphy characterization reduces claims, change orders, and bid costs through reduced contractor uncertainty.
key_points: Data report: factual only, no interpretations; may be legally binding part of bid documents
Design report: includes interpretations and recommendations; generally not in bid documents
GBR: contractually binding baseline for ground conditions in design-build projects
Financial benefits: reduced design conservatism, early hazard identification, reduced contractor risk and bid prices
